sections.title: PW-2: Playwright DOM, Locators, Selectors and Element Interactions
sections.body:
# PW-2: Playwright DOM, Locators, Selectors and Element Interactions

Playwright Masterclass · Python + TypeScript · Generative AI · Interview Preparation

In PW-1, we learned how Playwright launches browsers, creates isolated browser contexts, opens pages and performs basic automated testing.

Now we will learn the most fundamental skill in browser automation: **how to identify the correct element on a webpage and interact with it reliably.**

If you master locators, element interactions and synchronization, you will have a strong foundation for writing professional Playwright automation frameworks and AI-powered browser agents.

## Learning roadmap

| Concept | Interview priority |
|--------|--------|
| HTML, DOM and element attributes | Critical |
| Accessibility tree | Critical |
| CSS selectors | Critical |
| XPath selectors | High |
| Playwright locators | Critical |
| Role, text and label locators | Critical |
| Placeholder and test ID locators | High |
| Locator chaining and filtering | Critical |
| `has`, `hasText`, `first`, `last`, `nth` | Critical |
| Locator strictness | Critical |
| Locator vs ElementHandle | Critical |
| Click, double-click and fill | Critical |
| Keyboard and mouse operations | High |
| Checkboxes and radio buttons | High |
| Dropdowns and forms | Critical |
| Dynamic elements | Critical |
| AI-powered locator strategies | Critical |

**Allocated study time:** 1.5 hours in our accelerated interview preparation roadmap, with additional hands-on practice recommended.

sections.title: Understanding HTML and the DOM
sections.body:
## 1.1 Storytelling: Finding a person in a large company Imagine visiting a company with 5,000 employees. You need to find a software engineer named John. You could identify him using his name, employee ID, department, designation or office location. Similarly, a webpage contains hundreds or thousands of elements. Playwright needs a way to identify the exact element you want to interact with. Every element may have a tag name, ID, class, text, accessibility role, attributes and relationships with other elements. These properties help us locate it. ## 1.2 What is HTML? HTML describes the structure and content of a webpage. Consider a simple AI chatbot interface: ```html AI Chatbot

AI Assistant

``` The browser parses this HTML and creates an in-memory representation called the DOM. ## 1.3 What is the DOM? DOM stands for **Document Object Model**. It is a tree-like representation of the document that allows JavaScript and browser automation tools to inspect and manipulate elements. ## HTML document converted into a DOM tree Important relationships: | Relationship | Example | |--------|--------| | Parent | `form` is the parent of `input` | | Child | `button` is a child of `form` | | Sibling | `input` and `button` are siblings | | Ancestor | `body` is an ancestor of `button` | | Descendant | `button` is a descendant of `body` | | Root element | `html` | These relationships become particularly important when writing CSS selectors, XPath expressions and chained locators. ## 1.4 Understand an HTML element ```html ``` | Property | Value | |--------|--------| | Tag | `button` | | ID | `send-btn` | | Classes | `primary`, `large` | | Test ID | `send-button` | | Type | `submit` | | Visible text | `Send` | | Implicit accessibility role | `button` | All these properties can be used to identify the same element. ## 1.5 How to inspect elements in Chrome On a desktop browser, right-click an element and select **Inspect**, or open Developer Tools using `F12`. The Elements panel displays the DOM structure and element attributes. Do not automatically copy the long XPath or CSS selector suggested by Developer Tools. Those generated selectors can depend heavily on the current DOM structure and may break when the frontend changes. Instead, inspect the element and choose a stable locator.

sections.title: Accessibility tree
sections.body:
## 2.1 Storytelling: Identifying employees by responsibility

Imagine two employees:

- One is responsible for approving payments.
- Another is responsible for processing customer requests.

Instead of identifying them by their office furniture or clothing color, you identify them by their role and name.

Accessible locators use a similar principle.

Rather than locating a button using an arbitrary CSS class, we locate it based on what it represents to the user.

## 2.2 DOM tree vs accessibility tree

Browsers derive accessibility information from the DOM, rendering state and semantic attributes.

This information describes meaningful roles, accessible names, states and relationships.

**DOM representation**

div
  form
    label
    input
    button
  p

Document structure and implementation details.

**Accessibility representation**

document
  textbox "Question"
  button "Send"
  status

Semantic roles, names and user-facing meaning.

The accessibility representation is not necessarily a one-to-one copy of the DOM tree. Some DOM elements contribute semantics without appearing as independent accessible nodes.

## 2.3 Common accessibility roles

| HTML element | Typical role |
|--------|--------|
| `button` | button |
| `a` with href | link |
| `h1` through `h6` | heading |
| Text input | textbox |
| Checkbox input | checkbox |
| Radio input | radio |
| Ordinary single-select dropdown | combobox |
| `table` | table |
| `tr` | row |
| `nav` | navigation |
| `main` | main |
| Element with `role="status"` | status |

Some elements have different roles depending on their attributes and configuration.

## 2.4 Accessible names

Consider:

```html
<button>Send</button>
```

Role:

```text
button
```

Accessible name:

```text
Send
```

Another example:

```html
<button aria-label="Close dialog">
    X
</button>
```

The accessible name is generally `Close dialog`, not `X`.

Python:

```python
page.get_by_role(
    "button",
    name="Close dialog"
).click()
```

TypeScript:

```typescript
await page.getByRole(
    "button",
    { name: "Close dialog" }
).click();
```

Accessible names can come from labels, text content, ARIA attributes and other sources according to accessibility naming rules.

## 2.5 Why accessibility-based locators matter

Suppose the frontend changes from:

```html
<button class="blue-btn">Send</button>
```

to:

```html
<button class="rounded-primary">Send</button>
```

This CSS locator may break:

```typescript
page.locator(".blue-btn");
```

This semantic locator can continue working:

```typescript
page.getByRole("button", {
    name: "Send"
});
```

The implementation changed, but the user-facing purpose did not.

That is why semantic locators are often preferred for functional testing.

sections.title: CSS selectors
sections.body:
## 3.1 Storytelling: Finding a house using its address

Suppose you need to deliver a parcel.

You can identify a house using its house number, street name, building name or relationship to another building.

CSS selectors identify HTML elements using similar structural information.

Although CSS selectors were originally designed for styling HTML elements, browser automation frameworks also use them to locate elements.

## 3.2 Basic CSS selector syntax

Consider the following HTML:

```html
<form id="login-form">

    <input
        id="email"
        class="input-field"
        name="email"
        type="email"
    />

    <input
        id="password"
        class="input-field"
        name="password"
        type="password"
    />

    <button
        id="login-btn"
        class="primary"
        data-testid="login-button"
    >
        Login
    </button>

</form>
```

| Selector | Meaning |
|--------|--------|
| `input` | All input elements |
| `#email` | Element with ID email |
| `.input-field` | Elements with class input-field |
| `input.input-field` | Inputs with that class |
| `[name="email"]` | Elements with the specified name |
| `input[type="password"]` | Password inputs |
| `button.primary` | Buttons with class primary |
| `#login-form button` | Buttons inside login-form |
| `#login-form > button` | Direct button children |
| `[data-testid="login-button"]` | Element with the specified test ID |

## 3.3 Using CSS selectors in Playwright

### Python

```python
page.locator("#email").fill(
    "test@example.com"
)

page.locator("#password").fill(
    "test-password"
)

page.locator("#login-btn").click()
```

### TypeScript

```typescript
await page.locator("#email").fill(
    "test@example.com"
);

await page.locator("#password").fill(
    "test-password"
);

await page.locator("#login-btn").click();
```

The selector syntax is identical because both languages use the same Playwright selector engine.

## 3.4 CSS relationship selectors

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 340 215" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="95" y="5" width="150" height="35" rx="5" stroke="#2563eb" fill="#2563eb" fill-opacity=".08" /><text x="170" y="27" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">section.card</text><path d="M170 40 V60 H85 V80 M170 60 H255 V80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".5" fill="none" /><rect x="10" y="80" width="150" height="36" rx="5" stroke="#888" fill="#888" fill-opacity=".06" /><text x="85" y="102" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">div.content</text><rect x="180" y="80" width="150" height="36" rx="5" stroke="#0d9488" fill="#0d9488" fill-opacity=".08" /><text x="255" y="102" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">button: Delete</text><path d="M85 116 V151" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".5" /><rect x="10" y="151" width="150" height="36" rx="5" stroke="#0d9488" fill="#0d9488" fill-opacity=".08" /><text x="85" y="173" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">button: View</text><text x="255" y="139" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Direct child</text><text x="85" y="204" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">Nested descendant</text></svg>
```

`section button` matches both buttons.

`section > button` matches only Delete.

| Selector | Relationship |
|--------|--------|
| `A B` | B is a descendant of A |
| `A > B` | B is a direct child of A |
| `A + B` | B immediately follows sibling A |
| `A ~ B` | B follows sibling A under the same parent |
| `A, B` | Matches A or B |
| `A.class` | Element A has the specified class |

## 3.5 Advanced CSS attribute selectors

| Selector | Meaning |
|--------|--------|
| `[id="question"]` | Exact attribute value |
| `[id^="chat-"]` | Value starts with chat- |
| `[id$="-button"]` | Value ends with -button |
| `[id*="send"]` | Value contains send |
| `[disabled]` | Attribute exists |
| `input:checked` | Checked input |
| `button:not([disabled])` | Button without disabled attribute |

Playwright additionally supports selector extensions such as `:visible` and `:has-text()`. These are not all standard browser CSS selectors. 

## 3.6 Interactive CSS selector laboratory

## Find elements using CSS selectors

Choose a selectorCurrent selection unavailable.

Simulated chatbot DOM

Matching elements

Python

page.locator().count()

TypeScript

await page.locator().count()

This laboratory demonstrates predefined selectors against a simplified DOM.

## 3.7 Fragile vs reliable CSS selectors

Fragile:

```typescript
page.locator(
    "body > div:nth-child(2) > div > form > button"
);
```

More maintainable:

```typescript
page.locator("#send-btn");
```

User-oriented alternative:

```typescript
page.getByRole("button", {
    name: "Send"
});
```

A CSS selector is not inherently bad. A stable application-owned ID can be an excellent selector. The problem is depending unnecessarily on implementation details that change frequently.

sections.title: XPath selectors
sections.body:
## 4.1 Storytelling: Navigating a family tree Imagine tracing relationships through a family tree. You might identify a person by their parent, sibling, descendant or ancestor. XPath provides expressions for navigating document trees using similar relationships. XPath is especially useful when identifying elements through complex structural relationships, although semantic Playwright locators are often simpler. ## 4.2 Absolute vs relative XPath Absolute XPath: ```xpath /html/body/div/form/button ``` This depends on the full path through the document. Relative XPath: ```xpath //button[@id='login-btn'] ``` This searches for button elements with a particular attribute. Relative XPath is generally less dependent on the entire page structure. ## 4.3 Frequently used XPath expressions | XPath | Meaning | |--------|--------| | `//input` | All input elements | | `//input[@id='email']` | Input with ID email | | `//*[@id='email']` | Any element with ID email | | `//button[text()='Login']` | Button with matching direct text node | | `//button[normalize-space(.)='Login']` | Button with normalized matching string value | | `//button[contains(.,'Login')]` | Button containing Login text | | `//input[@type='password']` | Password input | | `//div[@id='chat']//button` | Descendant buttons | | `//form/button` | Direct button children of forms | | `(//button)[1]` | First button in the matched sequence | Remember that XPath positions are generally one-based, while Playwright's `nth()` uses zero-based indexing. ## 4.4 XPath axes Consider: ```html

RAG Documentation

``` Select the Delete button using its sibling heading: ```xpath //h3[normalize-space(.)='RAG Documentation'] /following-sibling::button ``` Select its parent: ```xpath //h3[normalize-space(.)='RAG Documentation'] /parent::div ``` Select an ancestor: ```xpath //h3/ancestor::div[@class='document-card'] ``` ## 4.5 Python and TypeScript implementation Python: ```python page.locator( "xpath=//input[@id='email']" ).fill("test@example.com") page.locator( "xpath=//button[normalize-space(.)='Login']" ).click() ``` TypeScript: ```typescript await page.locator( "xpath=//input[@id='email']" ).fill("test@example.com"); await page.locator( "xpath=//button[normalize-space(.)='Login']" ).click(); ``` ## 4.6 CSS vs XPath vs semantic locators | Capability | CSS | XPath | Semantic locator | |--------|--------|--------|--------| | Match ID or attribute | Yes | Yes | Through appropriate API | | Match text | Playwright extensions available | Yes | Yes | | Navigate ancestors | Possible with relational selectors | Explicit axes | Often handled through filtering | | Readability | Good for simple queries | Can become complex | Usually excellent | | User-facing semantics | Not inherently | Not inherently | Yes | | Open shadow DOM | Playwright CSS supports it | Does not pierce shadow roots | Generally supported | | Maintenance | Depends on selector | Depends on selector | Often more resilient | **Interview question:** Which is faster, CSS or XPath? A better answer is that performance depends on the browser, selector and document. For most E2E tests, reliability and clarity matter much more than small selector evaluation differences.
